questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.1: Design and implement response plans and runbooks to respond to security incidents.
questions.text: A GuardDuty finding indicates possible EC2 credential exfiltration. The security team wants a repeatable plan that analysts can execute consistently. What should the runbook define first?

answers.text: Triage steps, severity criteria, affected-resource identification, containment actions, and evidence preservation
Immediate termination of every EC2 instance in the account
Only a link to the GuardDuty console with no response steps
A request to disable CloudTrail during investigation

explanations.a: A useful incident runbook starts by turning the finding into a scoped, prioritized workflow that preserves evidence before destructive changes occur.
explanations.b: Account-wide termination can destroy evidence and disrupt unrelated workloads before scope is confirmed.
explanations.c: A console link helps navigation but does not define triage, ownership, containment, or evidence handling.
explanations.d: CloudTrail is needed for evidence and should not be disabled during an incident.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.1: Design and implement response plans and runbooks to respond to security incidents.
questions.text: A company has separate playbooks for public S3 bucket exposure, compromised IAM credentials, and suspicious container runtime activity. What should be standardized across all playbooks?

answers.text: The same containment command for every incident type
Roles, severity model, communication path, evidence handling, escalation triggers, and closure criteria
A requirement to wait for business hours before any response
A policy to delete raw evidence after summary writing

explanations.a: Different incidents require different containment actions, so one command can be unsafe.
explanations.b: Common response structure keeps incident execution consistent while allowing technical steps to differ by incident type.
explanations.c: Security incidents can require immediate action based on severity.
explanations.d: Evidence retention supports investigation, legal, and post-incident needs.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.1: Design and implement response plans and runbooks to respond to security incidents.
questions.text: A runbook for suspected IAM key compromise must support fast containment without losing attribution. Which step belongs in the runbook?

answers.text: Delete the IAM user and all CloudTrail records immediately
Rotate unrelated KMS keys before confirming the principal's actions
Deactivate the access key, preserve CloudTrail activity, and investigate recent API calls by the principal
Open administrator access to all responders by default

explanations.a: Deleting identity and audit records can remove evidence needed to determine impact.
explanations.b: Unrelated key rotation can add risk and does not scope the compromised IAM key.
explanations.c: Disabling the key limits further use while CloudTrail evidence identifies scope, actions, and resources affected.
explanations.d: Broad emergency access increases blast radius and is not tied to the compromised key response.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.1: Design and implement response plans and runbooks to respond to security incidents.
questions.text: A security team wants response plans for ransomware-like activity in an S3 data lake. Which runbook element is most important?

answers.text: Disable S3 Versioning after the first suspicious delete
Make the bucket public so external analysts can inspect it quickly
Delete lifecycle and access logs to reduce storage charges
Steps to isolate write paths, preserve object versions, review access logs, and validate clean recovery points

explanations.a: Versioning can preserve prior object versions and should not be removed during response.
explanations.b: Public access expands exposure and is not required for investigation.
explanations.c: Lifecycle and access evidence can help identify scope and attack timeline.
explanations.d: S3 ransomware response depends on stopping destructive writes, retaining object history, and recovering from trusted versions or backups.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.1: Design and implement response plans and runbooks to respond to security incidents.
questions.text: A team uses Systems Manager OpsCenter for incident work. What should a security incident response plan specify?

answers.text: How findings create OpsItems, required context fields, assignment, escalation, and linked automation documents
Use OpsCenter only as a generic bookmark folder
Place production credentials in OpsItem descriptions
Create OpsItems manually only after all remediation is complete

explanations.a: OpsCenter is most effective when incident intake, ownership, context, and automation links are defined before incidents occur.
explanations.b: Generic bookmarks do not provide incident ownership, status, or response workflow.
explanations.c: Incident records must not expose secrets.
explanations.d: Late record creation loses timeline and decision evidence during response.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.1: Design and implement response plans and runbooks to respond to security incidents.
questions.text: A runbook for AI application abuse must address prompt injection and unsafe output attempts. What should it include?

answers.text: Store every user prompt publicly for community analysis
Detection inputs, guardrail outcomes, abuse-scoping steps, model access review, and safe evidence handling
Treat all model refusals as successful attacks
Disable all application authentication to reproduce abuse

explanations.a: Prompts can contain sensitive data and must be handled under evidence controls.
explanations.b: GenAI incident response needs application-specific evidence, control outcomes, and user or identity scope without overcollecting sensitive prompts.
explanations.c: Refusals can show controls working and need context before severity is assigned.
explanations.d: Removing authentication changes conditions and can expose the application further.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.1: Design and implement response plans and runbooks to respond to security incidents.
questions.text: A regulated organization wants runbooks that auditors can review. What design requirement matters most?

answers.text: Runbooks edited only in an untracked chat thread
A plan that depends entirely on one engineer's memory
Version-controlled runbooks with approvals, test history, and mapped evidence requirements
A single emergency role with no logging requirement

explanations.a: Chat edits lack durable review, versioning, and approval history.
explanations.b: Knowledge in one person's memory cannot be audited or reliably executed.
explanations.c: Auditable runbooks need change history, governance, and proof that procedures are tested and aligned to evidence needs.
explanations.d: Emergency access still needs monitoring and evidence.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.1: Design and implement response plans and runbooks to respond to security incidents.
questions.text: A security team wants a runbook for a compromised EKS workload. Which response plan element is most specific to Kubernetes workloads?

answers.text: Only review Route 53 domain registration records
Immediately delete the entire cluster with no evidence capture
Rotate every unrelated database credential before scoping the workload
Preserve pod logs and Kubernetes audit context, isolate the workload, and review service account permissions

explanations.a: Domain registration does not identify compromised pod behavior or service account use.
explanations.b: Cluster deletion can destroy evidence and create unnecessary outage.
explanations.c: Unscoped rotation can disrupt services without addressing the Kubernetes evidence path.
explanations.d: EKS incidents require container and cluster context in addition to AWS account evidence.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.1: Design and implement response plans and runbooks to respond to security incidents.
questions.text: A response plan for suspected data exfiltration needs a decision point for customer notification. What should the runbook capture before that decision?

answers.text: Confirmed data types, affected resources, access path, time window, identities, and legal or compliance contacts
Only the first analyst's opinion that the event looks serious
Only the total number of CloudWatch dashboards
A plan to destroy all logs after contacting customers

explanations.a: Notification decisions require scoped evidence about what data was accessed, how, when, and who must be involved.
explanations.b: Opinions must be supported by evidence before external notification decisions.
explanations.c: Dashboard count has no bearing on exfiltration scope or notification duties.
explanations.d: That logs remain needed for investigation, reporting, and post-incident actions.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.1: Design and implement response plans and runbooks to respond to security incidents.
questions.text: A team wants every high-severity incident runbook to support rapid handoff between shifts. Which section is essential?

answers.text: A blank template that responders fill in after closure
Current state summary, completed actions, open hypotheses, evidence locations, and next decisions
Only a list of AWS service names with no actions
A requirement that the original responder stay online indefinitely

explanations.a: Closure-only documentation does not help active handoff.
explanations.b: Shift handoff needs operational context that prevents repeated work and preserves decision continuity.
explanations.c: Service names alone do not convey investigation state or decisions.
explanations.d: Response plans should work across shifts without depending on one responder.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.2: Use AWS service features and capabilities to configure services to be prepared for incidents.
questions.text: A company wants to be ready to isolate compromised EC2 instances without needing inbound SSH. Which preparation is most appropriate?

answers.text: Open SSH from the internet to every instance for emergency access
Wait to create instance roles until after a compromise
Configure Systems Manager Session Manager, instance profiles, and preapproved isolation security groups
Store administrator passwords in user data for responders

explanations.a: Broad SSH exposure increases attack surface and is not required for managed response.
explanations.b: Roles and access paths should be ready before incidents to avoid delay.
explanations.c: Incident readiness requires managed access, authorized automation, and containment controls before a compromise occurs.
explanations.d: User data is not a secure emergency credential store.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.2: Use AWS service features and capabilities to configure services to be prepared for incidents.
questions.text: A public application is protected by AWS Shield Advanced. What incident-readiness capability should be configured before a DDoS event?

answers.text: Enable Shield Advanced only after the attack saturates the application
Remove all CloudWatch alarms to reduce noise during attack periods
Make origin servers public and bypass edge protections
Health-based detection, protected resources, contacts, and response engagement procedures

explanations.a: Late enablement can delay protection and response engagement.
explanations.b: Alarms help distinguish attack impact and recovery status.
explanations.c: Bypassing edge controls can increase exposure during DDoS events.
explanations.d: Shield Advanced readiness depends on protected resource configuration and clear escalation paths before attack traffic begins.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.2: Use AWS service features and capabilities to configure services to be prepared for incidents.
questions.text: A security account must investigate member accounts during incidents. What access should be provisioned in advance?

answers.text: Cross-account investigation roles with least-privilege read and containment permissions
Root credentials for all member accounts in a shared document
A request process that starts only after a critical incident begins
Public resource policies for all logs and snapshots

explanations.a: Preprovisioned roles reduce response delay while preserving account boundaries and auditability.
explanations.b: Root credential sharing is unsafe and unnecessary for investigations.
explanations.c: Starting access provisioning during an incident can miss response objectives.
explanations.d: Public access to evidence or resources creates additional security risk.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.2: Use AWS service features and capabilities to configure services to be prepared for incidents.
questions.text: A company wants forensic readiness for compromised EC2 instances. Which preparation should be implemented?

answers.text: Store forensic evidence on the suspect instance only
Automated snapshot and memory-safe evidence workflows with dedicated evidence storage and access controls
Give every developer delete permissions on evidence buckets
Disable timestamps in logs to save space

explanations.a: Evidence kept only on the suspect host can be altered or lost.
explanations.b: Forensic readiness depends on repeatable capture, protected storage, and controlled access to evidence.
explanations.c: Broad delete access can compromise evidence integrity.
explanations.d: Timestamps are essential for forensic timelines.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.2: Use AWS service features and capabilities to configure services to be prepared for incidents.
questions.text: A workload uses AWS Backup for critical data. What incident-readiness configuration supports recovery after destructive activity?

answers.text: Backups stored only in the same account with broad delete permissions
Untested backups with no restore runbook
Protected backup vaults, tested restores, cross-account or cross-Region copies, and locked retention where required
A plan to rebuild all data manually from application logs

explanations.a: Same-account broad delete rights can allow an attacker to remove recovery points.
explanations.b: Backup completion does not prove recovery works during an incident.
explanations.c: Prepared recovery needs resilient backups that survive account compromise and have proven restore procedures.
explanations.d: Application logs are usually incomplete for full data recovery.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.2: Use AWS service features and capabilities to configure services to be prepared for incidents.
questions.text: A security incident response team needs to analyze suspicious activity in SageMaker AI notebooks. What readiness control should exist?

answers.text: Disable all notebook logging because notebooks are interactive
Let all notebooks run with administrator roles by default
Store investigation results in the notebook's temporary directory only
Preapproved investigation access, notebook activity logging, network controls, and data access auditing

explanations.a: Interactive use still needs auditability for security response.
explanations.b: Broad roles increase blast radius and complicate incident scoping.
explanations.c: Temporary local storage is not durable evidence handling.
explanations.d: Notebook incident readiness requires visibility into code execution, data access, identity, and network paths.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.2: Use AWS service features and capabilities to configure services to be prepared for incidents.
questions.text: A company wants to minimize blast radius when an incident affects one workload account. Which preparation supports this?

answers.text: Use separate accounts, scoped roles, SCPs, and isolated logging and backup administration
Run all workloads, logs, and backups in one unrestricted account
Grant every workload role access to every account for convenience
Use one shared KMS key administrator role for all teams with no monitoring

explanations.a: Account and permission isolation reduce the chance that one workload incident spreads to governance, logs, or backups.
explanations.b: Shared unrestricted administration increases blast radius.
explanations.c: Broad cross-account access expands impact of a compromised role.
explanations.d: Shared key administration makes containment and attribution harder.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.2: Use AWS service features and capabilities to configure services to be prepared for incidents.
questions.text: A team wants to use Automated Forensics Orchestrator for Amazon EC2 during incidents. What must be prepared?

answers.text: Install the tool only after deleting the affected instance
Deployment, permissions, evidence destinations, and invocation procedures for the orchestrator
Allow the tool to write evidence to public buckets
Run the tool with no IAM permissions

explanations.a: Deleting the instance first can remove evidence that the orchestrator needs.
explanations.b: Automated forensic tools require preconfigured roles and storage so they can collect evidence safely when triggered.
explanations.c: Forensic evidence should be protected from public access.
explanations.d: The orchestrator needs scoped permissions to collect and store evidence.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.2: Use AWS service features and capabilities to configure services to be prepared for incidents.
questions.text: A company uses Application Recovery Controller for critical applications. How does it support incident preparedness?

answers.text: It replaces the need for security logging
It automatically writes every application runbook
It can provide readiness checks and controlled routing actions for recovery scenarios
It scans container images for vulnerabilities

explanations.a: Recovery orchestration does not replace audit and detection logs.
explanations.b: Runbook design remains a human and governance responsibility.
explanations.c: Application Recovery Controller helps prepare and coordinate recovery by evaluating readiness and controlling traffic shift decisions.
explanations.d: Container image scanning is an Inspector use case, not an Application Recovery Controller function.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.2: Use AWS service features and capabilities to configure services to be prepared for incidents.
questions.text: A security team must respond to high-severity events outside business hours. What service configuration improves readiness?

answers.text: A dashboard that is reviewed during quarterly meetings
One personal email address with no backup contact
Unrouted findings stored only in each workload account
On-call notifications, escalation policies, and tested contact paths integrated with alarms and findings

explanations.a: Quarterly review does not support urgent response.
explanations.b: Single-contact notification can fail when that person is unavailable.
explanations.c: Unrouted findings delay security operations response.
explanations.d: High-severity incidents require working notification and escalation paths before responders are needed.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.3: Recommend procedures to test and validate the effectiveness of an incident response plan.
questions.text: A company wants to verify that its compromised-key runbook works without exposing production credentials. What test is appropriate?

answers.text: Run a tabletop or controlled simulation using test keys and validate detection, containment, and evidence steps
Expose a real production access key publicly to see what happens
Only ask responders if they remember the runbook title
Skip testing because the runbook is written clearly

explanations.a: A controlled test exercises the response process without risking real production credentials.
explanations.b: Intentionally exposing production credentials creates unacceptable risk.
explanations.c: Recall of a title does not validate the technical response workflow.
explanations.d: Documentation quality does not prove that detection and containment steps work.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.3: Recommend procedures to test and validate the effectiveness of an incident response plan.
questions.text: A security team wants to test whether responders can isolate a compromised EC2 instance. Which validation should be included?

answers.text: Read the security group policy aloud during a meeting
Execute a game day that applies isolation controls to a test instance and verifies connectivity is blocked
Delete a random production instance to create urgency
Run only a cost report for the test account

explanations.a: Discussion does not prove the control works on an instance.
explanations.b: Testing containment must prove that the isolation control changes the network state as intended.
explanations.c: Destructive production testing can cause avoidable outage and evidence loss.
explanations.d: Cost reporting does not validate instance isolation.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.3: Recommend procedures to test and validate the effectiveness of an incident response plan.
questions.text: A response plan depends on restoring clean backups after destructive S3 activity. What test validates the plan?

answers.text: Check only that a backup job has a green status
Delete all previous versions from production before the test
Restore selected objects or datasets into an isolated environment and verify integrity and access controls
Open restored data publicly for easy validation

explanations.a: Backup success does not prove restore usability.
explanations.b: Removing versions can destroy recovery options.
explanations.c: Backup response plans need proof that restored data is complete, clean, and protected.
explanations.d: Public restore validation can expose sensitive data.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.3: Recommend procedures to test and validate the effectiveness of an incident response plan.
questions.text: A tabletop exercise found that responders could not find the right evidence bucket. What improvement should be made?

answers.text: Ignore the result because tabletop exercises do not matter
Create more evidence buckets without naming standards
Delete evidence storage from the response process
Update the runbook, evidence inventory, and test checklist, then retest discovery of evidence locations

explanations.a: Tabletop failures reveal operational gaps before real incidents.
explanations.b: More unclear locations worsen discovery problems.
explanations.c: Evidence storage remains necessary for investigation and audit.
explanations.d: Incident response validation should feed specific corrections and verify that the correction works.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.3: Recommend procedures to test and validate the effectiveness of an incident response plan.
questions.text: A company wants to test incident response for a degraded multi-Region application. Which AWS service can inject controlled failures?

answers.text: AWS Fault Injection Service
AWS Certificate Manager
Amazon Macie
AWS CodeArtifact

explanations.a: Fault Injection Service can run controlled experiments that validate resilience and response procedures.
explanations.b: ACM manages certificates and does not inject system failures.
explanations.c: Macie discovers sensitive S3 data and does not run failure experiments.
explanations.d: CodeArtifact stores packages and does not test recovery behavior.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.3: Recommend procedures to test and validate the effectiveness of an incident response plan.
questions.text: A resilience review needs to determine whether recovery procedures meet application objectives. Which service can assess resilience posture?

answers.text: Amazon Cognito user pools
AWS Resilience Hub
S3 Object Lambda
Amazon ECR pull-through cache

explanations.a: Cognito manages user authentication and does not assess application resilience posture.
explanations.b: Resilience Hub can assess applications against resilience objectives and help identify gaps.
explanations.c: Object Lambda transforms S3 object responses and does not assess incident response effectiveness.
explanations.d: Pull-through cache helps image retrieval and does not validate recovery objectives.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.3: Recommend procedures to test and validate the effectiveness of an incident response plan.
questions.text: A production incident test must avoid customer impact. What procedure should be used?

answers.text: Run uncontrolled failure injection against every production resource at peak time
Disable monitoring during the exercise
Run tests in a representative isolated environment or use scoped experiments with clear abort criteria
Keep test goals secret from all responders after execution starts

explanations.a: Unbounded production testing can cause outages.
explanations.b: Monitoring is required to measure detection and response behavior.
explanations.c: Safe validation limits blast radius while still exercising the response plan.
explanations.d: Responders need defined exercise rules, safety boundaries, and communication paths.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.3: Recommend procedures to test and validate the effectiveness of an incident response plan.
questions.text: An organization wants evidence that its incident response plan improves over time. What should each test produce?

answers.text: Only a celebratory message that the test happened
A list of people who attended with no technical findings
Deletion of all exercise logs to avoid embarrassment
Measured results, gaps, owners, due dates, and follow-up validation

explanations.a: A message without results or actions does not prove improvement.
explanations.b: Attendance does not show whether the response plan works.
explanations.c: Exercise logs support learning and audit evidence.
explanations.d: Testing creates value when findings become tracked improvements with accountable verification.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.3: Recommend procedures to test and validate the effectiveness of an incident response plan.
questions.text: A security team wants to validate a GenAI abuse response plan. What should the exercise include?

answers.text: Simulated prompt injection or data exfiltration attempts with guardrail, logging, escalation, and evidence checks
Only a generic EC2 reboot exercise
Logging all real customer prompts in plaintext for test data
Disabling guardrails before testing response

explanations.a: GenAI incident testing should exercise the specific controls and evidence paths used for model abuse scenarios.
explanations.b: EC2 reboot testing does not validate prompt, guardrail, and model access response paths.
explanations.c: Real customer prompt capture can create privacy and confidentiality issues.
explanations.d: Testing should validate guardrail behavior, not remove the control being assessed.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.3: Recommend procedures to test and validate the effectiveness of an incident response plan.
questions.text: A response exercise shows the incident commander role is unclear. What should be updated?

answers.text: Only the color of the incident dashboard
The response plan's roles, decision authority, escalation path, and communication protocol
The backup retention policy only
The names of unrelated IAM users

explanations.a: Dashboard styling does not assign authority or escalation.
explanations.b: Role clarity prevents conflicting actions and supports faster coordinated response.
explanations.c: Backup retention does not resolve incident command ambiguity.
explanations.d: Unrelated identity names do not define response leadership.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.4: Use AWS services to automatically remediate incidents.
questions.text: A GuardDuty finding indicates an EC2 instance is communicating with a command-and-control domain. What automated remediation is appropriate after validation criteria are met?

answers.text: Immediately delete the instance and all logs
Add an inbound rule that allows all internet traffic
Trigger a Systems Manager or Lambda workflow that applies an isolation security group and captures evidence
Disable GuardDuty to stop repeated alerts

explanations.a: Deletion can destroy evidence needed to scope the compromise.
explanations.b: Opening access increases exposure instead of containment.
explanations.c: Automated isolation can contain network activity while evidence capture preserves data for investigation.
explanations.d: Disabling detection removes visibility into ongoing threat activity.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.4: Use AWS services to automatically remediate incidents.
questions.text: A public S3 bucket exposure finding should be remediated automatically when the bucket is not approved for public access. Which action fits?

answers.text: Delete the bucket without owner review
Publish a copy of the bucket policy in a public issue
Ignore the finding when the bucket contains many objects
Apply Block Public Access or a restrictive bucket policy and record the previous policy state

explanations.a: Bucket deletion can cause data loss and may not be appropriate for every exposure.
explanations.b: Public issue content can expose sensitive policy and resource details.
explanations.c: Object count does not make public exposure acceptable.
explanations.d: Automated S3 containment should remove unintended exposure while preserving before-state evidence.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.4: Use AWS services to automatically remediate incidents.
questions.text: A Config rule detects security groups that allow unrestricted SSH. Which automated remediation design is appropriate?

answers.text: Invoke Systems Manager Automation or Lambda to remove the rule after confirming scope and exception status
Remove every inbound rule from every security group
Create another unrestricted SSH rule with a different description
Disable AWS Config to stop noncompliance events

explanations.a: Security group remediation should validate the target and approved exceptions before changing access.
explanations.b: Broad rule removal can break unrelated applications.
explanations.c: A second unrestricted rule preserves the exposure.
explanations.d: Removing detection leaves the risky configuration in place.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.4: Use AWS services to automatically remediate incidents.
questions.text: A malicious access key is confirmed. Which automatic containment step is safest?

answers.text: Delete all CloudTrail logs containing the key ID
Deactivate the access key and notify the owner while preserving CloudTrail evidence
Leave the key active until the next rotation cycle
Grant the same key administrator access for easier tracing

explanations.a: Audit records are necessary for determining what the key did.
explanations.b: Deactivation stops further API use without deleting identity context needed for investigation.
explanations.c: A confirmed malicious key should be contained quickly.
explanations.d: Increasing permissions expands attacker capability.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.4: Use AWS services to automatically remediate incidents.
questions.text: A remediation workflow must coordinate several steps: isolate a host, snapshot volumes, tag evidence, and notify responders. Which service is best suited to orchestrate the workflow?

answers.text: AWS Certificate Manager
Amazon EFS lifecycle management
AWS Step Functions
Route 53 hosted zone comments

explanations.a: ACM manages certificates and does not orchestrate incident response workflows.
explanations.b: EFS lifecycle policies manage storage classes and not multi-step remediation.
explanations.c: Step Functions can coordinate multiple AWS service calls, branching, retries, and status tracking for remediation.
explanations.d: Hosted zone comments cannot coordinate response actions.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.4: Use AWS services to automatically remediate incidents.
questions.text: A remediation Lambda acts on Security Hub findings from multiple accounts. What permission model is required?

answers.text: Store root credentials for every account in Lambda environment variables
Allow the Lambda function to act without any IAM role
Make all member account resources public during remediation
A delegated automation role that assumes scoped remediation roles in target accounts

explanations.a: Root credential storage is unsafe and unnecessary.
explanations.b: AWS API remediation requires authorized credentials.
explanations.c: Public access is not a valid authorization model.
explanations.d: Cross-account remediation needs auditable trust and least-privilege target-account permissions.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.4: Use AWS services to automatically remediate incidents.
questions.text: Automated remediation sometimes acts on false positive findings. What guardrail should be added?

answers.text: Confidence thresholds, exception checks, approval gates for high-impact changes, and rollback steps
Remove all validation to make remediation faster
Run destructive actions first and review later
Suppress all findings from the affected service forever

explanations.a: Remediation automation needs safeguards so uncertain or destructive actions do not harm production.
explanations.b: Speed without validation increases the chance of damaging false-positive response.
explanations.c: Destructive response should be gated by confidence and recovery controls.
explanations.d: Global suppression creates a detection blind spot.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.4: Use AWS services to automatically remediate incidents.
questions.text: A recovery workflow must fail over an application when a regional security event affects the primary Region. Which service can provide routing controls for recovery readiness?

answers.text: AWS CodeArtifact
Amazon Application Recovery Controller
Amazon Macie
AWS CloudHSM

explanations.a: CodeArtifact stores packages and does not coordinate regional recovery routing.
explanations.b: Application Recovery Controller supports readiness and routing control patterns for application recovery scenarios.
explanations.c: Macie discovers sensitive data and does not shift application traffic.
explanations.d: CloudHSM provides dedicated HSMs and does not manage application failover routing.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.1.4: Use AWS services to automatically remediate incidents.
questions.text: A Systems Manager Automation document remediates incidents but leaves no record in the incident system. What improvement is needed?

answers.text: Suppress all execution output
Rename the document after every run
Emit execution status, parameters, resource IDs, and results to the incident record
Only send a message that says done

explanations.a: Missing output makes incident review and audit harder.
explanations.b: Renaming does not preserve execution details.
explanations.c: Automated remediation should preserve response evidence so investigators can understand what changed and whether it worked.
explanations.d: A generic completion message lacks target, action, and outcome details.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.1: Capture and store relevant system and application logs as forensic artifacts.
questions.text: An EC2 instance is suspected of compromise. Which logs should be captured as forensic artifacts before rebuilding if feasible?

answers.text: Only the current CPU utilization graph
Only the AMI name used by the instance
Only the latest deployment approval comment
Instance system logs, application logs, security agent logs, VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail events, and relevant snapshots

explanations.a: CPU graphs can show symptoms but are not enough for forensic reconstruction.
explanations.b: The AMI name does not preserve activity from the suspected compromise.
explanations.c: Approval comments do not capture runtime or control-plane evidence.
explanations.d: Forensic artifacts should cover host behavior, application activity, network traffic, API actions, and disk state.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.1: Capture and store relevant system and application logs as forensic artifacts.
questions.text: A container workload is compromised and pods are being replaced quickly. What evidence should be preserved?

answers.text: Container logs, Kubernetes audit events, pod specifications, image digests, and relevant runtime findings
Only the final desired replica count
Only a screenshot of the cluster overview
Only the developer's local kubeconfig file

explanations.a: Ephemeral containers require prompt preservation of logs, workload definitions, image identity, and cluster audit context.
explanations.b: Replica count does not explain what the compromised containers did.
explanations.c: Screenshots are not sufficient forensic artifacts.
explanations.d: A local kubeconfig does not preserve runtime evidence from the workload.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.1: Capture and store relevant system and application logs as forensic artifacts.
questions.text: A Lambda function is suspected of processing malicious payloads. Which artifacts should be captured?

answers.text: Only the Lambda function description
CloudWatch Logs, invocation request identifiers, function configuration, version or alias, and related CloudTrail events
Only the zip file size
Only DNS records for the application domain

explanations.a: The description does not preserve invocation or change evidence.
explanations.b: Serverless evidence includes execution logs, configuration, deployed version context, and API activity around changes.
explanations.c: Package size does not show malicious payload processing or configuration changes.
explanations.d: DNS records do not capture Lambda execution evidence.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.1: Capture and store relevant system and application logs as forensic artifacts.
questions.text: A security team stores forensic artifacts in S3. What storage controls are appropriate?

answers.text: Public read access so all employees can review evidence
Lifecycle expiration after one hour for all evidence
Dedicated evidence bucket with encryption, versioning, Object Lock where required, and restricted access
Unencrypted storage with broad delete permissions

explanations.a: Public access exposes sensitive evidence.
explanations.b: Very short retention can destroy needed forensic records.
explanations.c: Forensic artifacts need integrity, confidentiality, and retention controls that limit alteration or deletion.
explanations.d: Unencrypted broadly deletable evidence undermines forensic integrity.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.1: Capture and store relevant system and application logs as forensic artifacts.
questions.text: During an IAM compromise investigation, which CloudTrail data should be captured?

answers.text: Only successful application health checks
Only S3 lifecycle configuration for unrelated buckets
Only a list of CloudWatch dashboard names
Events for the suspected principal, source IPs, assumed roles, session context, and affected resources

explanations.a: Health checks do not show IAM activity.
explanations.b: Unrelated lifecycle settings do not scope identity compromise.
explanations.c: Dashboard names do not preserve API activity evidence.
explanations.d: CloudTrail context helps determine who acted, from where, through which session, and what was changed or accessed.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.1: Capture and store relevant system and application logs as forensic artifacts.
questions.text: A compromised database host may contain volatile evidence, but responders must avoid logging in interactively and changing state. What approach is appropriate?

answers.text: Use preapproved forensic automation to capture snapshots and relevant logs with minimal host interaction
Let multiple responders browse the host manually without recording commands
Patch and reboot the host before capturing anything
Delete all local logs to reduce attacker access

explanations.a: Automated evidence collection reduces unnecessary changes while preserving artifacts for analysis.
explanations.b: Untracked interactive access can alter evidence and complicate chain of custody.
explanations.c: Rebooting and patching can destroy volatile evidence and change system state.
explanations.d: Deleting logs destroys forensic evidence.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.1: Capture and store relevant system and application logs as forensic artifacts.
questions.text: A forensic workflow captures VPC Flow Logs but not application logs. What gap remains?

answers.text: Application logs are never useful in security incidents
Network metadata may show connections, but application-level actions and identities can be missing
VPC Flow Logs contain every HTTP header and request body
Flow logs automatically preserve disk state

explanations.a: Application logs often show user, request, and error context.
explanations.b: Flow logs and application logs answer different forensic questions and should be combined where relevant.
explanations.c: Flow logs contain metadata, not full layer 7 payloads.
explanations.d: Disk state requires snapshots or other host evidence collection.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.1: Capture and store relevant system and application logs as forensic artifacts.
questions.text: A legal hold is issued for incident evidence. What should the storage process do?

answers.text: Delete the artifacts immediately to reduce liability
Move evidence to a public bucket for visibility
Prevent expiration or deletion of the relevant artifacts and record the hold decision
Compress the artifacts and remove all timestamps

explanations.a: Deleting evidence under hold can violate legal or compliance requirements.
explanations.b: Public exposure is not required and can create additional risk.
explanations.c: Legal holds require retention controls that override ordinary lifecycle cleanup for scoped evidence.
explanations.d: Timestamps are essential to investigation timelines.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.1: Capture and store relevant system and application logs as forensic artifacts.
questions.text: An incident response team must share evidence with an external forensics provider. What access pattern is safest?

answers.text: Share the log archive root credentials
Make the entire evidence bucket public
Email every raw artifact to personal addresses
Time-bounded, least-privilege access to copied evidence with audit logging

explanations.a: Root credential sharing creates excessive account-wide risk.
explanations.b: Public access exposes unrelated evidence and sensitive data.
explanations.c: Personal email transfer is hard to govern and audit.
explanations.d: External evidence sharing should limit scope and duration while preserving an access record.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.2: Search and correlate logs for security events across applications and AWS services.
questions.text: A suspected compromised IAM role was used to access S3 and KMS. Which correlation approach should an analyst use?

answers.text: Join CloudTrail role session events, S3 data events, and KMS events by principal, time, and resource
Review only EC2 CPU metrics for the account
Search only for the role name in deployment notes
Ignore KMS events because encryption prevents abuse

explanations.a: Cross-service correlation reveals what the role session accessed and which encryption keys were used.
explanations.b: CPU metrics do not identify IAM role activity or data access.
explanations.c: Notes do not provide authoritative API activity.
explanations.d: KMS usage can show access to encrypted data and is important to scope.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.2: Search and correlate logs for security events across applications and AWS services.
questions.text: A suspicious web request appears in AWS WAF logs and the application later returned an error. How should logs be correlated?

answers.text: Compare only bucket storage class names
Match client IP, timestamp, host, URI, request ID if present, and downstream application logs
Use the CloudFormation stack description as the request ID
Delete the WAF logs after checking the application log

explanations.a: Storage classes do not correlate web requests.
explanations.b: Layer 7 investigation needs edge and application context connected by request attributes and time.
explanations.c: Stack descriptions do not identify individual requests.
explanations.d: WAF logs remain useful to understand rule matches and request shape.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.2: Search and correlate logs for security events across applications and AWS services.
questions.text: A GuardDuty finding reports unusual DNS exfiltration behavior. Which logs should be searched together?

answers.text: Only CodeBuild unit test reports
Only ECR lifecycle events
Route 53 Resolver query logs, VPC Flow Logs, CloudTrail events, and workload logs for the affected resource
Only AWS Billing console visits

explanations.a: Build tests do not explain runtime DNS exfiltration.
explanations.b: Image cleanup events do not show DNS or network activity.
explanations.c: DNS findings require domain lookup evidence, network paths, API context, and workload behavior.
explanations.d: Billing visits do not scope DNS exfiltration.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.2: Search and correlate logs for security events across applications and AWS services.
questions.text: An analyst has a Security Hub finding for a public S3 bucket. What cross-source evidence helps confirm impact?

answers.text: Only the number of objects in unrelated buckets
Only Lambda concurrency for backend functions
Only the source repository branch name
Security Hub finding details, S3 bucket policy, Block Public Access state, CloudTrail data events, and Macie findings

explanations.a: Unrelated buckets do not validate the affected bucket's exposure or data.
explanations.b: Lambda concurrency does not show S3 public exposure.
explanations.c: Branch name does not confirm bucket access or sensitive data.
explanations.d: Public bucket impact depends on exposure configuration, observed object access, and sensitivity of stored data.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.2: Search and correlate logs for security events across applications and AWS services.
questions.text: A container image vulnerability finding appears after a suspicious runtime event. What should be correlated?

answers.text: Inspector finding, image digest, deployed task or pod, runtime findings, and deployment history
Only Route 53 hosted zone counts
Only the account password policy age
Only S3 replication status

explanations.a: Image identity and deployment history connect vulnerability data to the affected running workload.
explanations.b: Hosted zone count does not connect an image finding to runtime exposure.
explanations.c: Password policy age does not identify affected containers.
explanations.d: Replication status does not map image vulnerabilities to deployed workloads.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.2: Search and correlate logs for security events across applications and AWS services.
questions.text: A login anomaly is reported for a federated user. What logs should be searched?

answers.text: Only VPC Flow Logs for database subnets
Identity provider logs, IAM Identity Center or role assumption records, CloudTrail activity, and application access logs
Only KMS key rotation history
Only CloudFront cache invalidations

explanations.a: Network metadata alone does not identify federated login context.
explanations.b: Federated identity investigations require both corporate identity context and AWS session activity.
explanations.c: Key rotation history does not show human login activity.
explanations.d: Cache invalidations do not scope federated user activity.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.2: Search and correlate logs for security events across applications and AWS services.
questions.text: A threat hunt looks for lateral movement across accounts. Which evidence should be correlated?

answers.text: Only the count of enabled Availability Zones
Only S3 lifecycle transition dates
AssumeRole events, source identities, target accounts, API actions, and network activity around the same times
Only application release version names

explanations.a: Availability Zone count does not reveal cross-account identity movement.
explanations.b: Lifecycle transitions do not show role chaining or API behavior.
explanations.c: Lateral movement in AWS often appears as role assumption followed by activity in multiple accounts.
explanations.d: Release names alone do not identify cross-account actions.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.2: Search and correlate logs for security events across applications and AWS services.
questions.text: A suspicious API call occurred at 12:03 UTC, but application logs use local time. What should the analyst normalize?

answers.text: Resource names by alphabetical order
Dashboard titles by team preference
Object storage class names
Timestamps and time zones before building the event timeline

explanations.a: Alphabetical ordering does not align events in time.
explanations.b: Dashboard titles do not create an accurate timeline.
explanations.c: Storage classes do not correct time comparisons.
explanations.d: Time normalization prevents false conclusions when correlating logs from different systems.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.2: Search and correlate logs for security events across applications and AWS services.
questions.text: A security event spans CloudTrail Lake, CloudWatch Logs, and Athena queries over S3 logs. What practice improves reproducibility?

answers.text: Save queries, time ranges, filters, and result references in the incident record
Only paste a vague note that logs looked suspicious
Delete query results after making a decision
Use unbounded queries with no time range for every incident

explanations.a: Reproducible investigations require the exact query context and evidence references used for conclusions.
explanations.b: Vague notes cannot be independently reviewed or rerun.
explanations.c: Results and references support validation and audit.
explanations.d: Unbounded queries are inefficient and hard to reproduce precisely.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.3: Validate findings from AWS security services to assess the scope and impact of an event.
questions.text: GuardDuty reports CryptoCurrency:EC2/BitcoinTool.B!DNS for an instance. What should the analyst do before containment?

answers.text: Dismiss the finding because GuardDuty can never be actionable
Validate the affected instance, DNS activity, recent changes, and business context to assess scope and urgency
Terminate every instance in the Region immediately
Disable DNS logging to reduce false positives

explanations.a: GuardDuty findings can indicate real threats and require triage.
explanations.b: Findings need confirmation and context so containment is targeted and proportional.
explanations.c: Region-wide termination is disproportionate before scope is understood.
explanations.d: DNS evidence is needed to validate the finding.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.3: Validate findings from AWS security services to assess the scope and impact of an event.
questions.text: Security Hub reports an RDS database is publicly accessible. How should scope and impact be assessed?

answers.text: Only check whether the database name is long
Assume encryption at rest eliminates all risk
Review database exposure, security groups, route paths, authentication logs, data sensitivity, and recent access
Close the finding because RDS generated no CPU alarm

explanations.a: Name length does not determine exposure or impact.
explanations.b: Encryption at rest does not prevent authorized or exposed network access.
explanations.c: Impact depends on whether the database is reachable, what data it holds, and whether suspicious access occurred.
explanations.d: CPU state does not validate public accessibility risk.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.3: Validate findings from AWS security services to assess the scope and impact of an event.
questions.text: Macie finds credentials in an S3 object. What validation step is most important?

answers.text: Post the credentials to a team channel for testing
Ignore the finding if the bucket is encrypted
Delete the finding without checking credential status
Determine whether the credentials are active, where the object is exposed, and whether the credentials were accessed

explanations.a: Sharing credentials further increases the risk.
explanations.b: Encryption at rest does not make exposed credentials harmless.
explanations.c: Closing the finding leaves potential active credentials unhandled.
explanations.d: Scope depends on secret validity, object exposure, and evidence of access or use.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.3: Validate findings from AWS security services to assess the scope and impact of an event.
questions.text: Inspector reports a critical container vulnerability. How should impact be validated?

answers.text: Map the vulnerable image digest to deployed workloads and evaluate exploitability, exposure, and compensating controls
Assume every scanned image is running in production
Ignore the finding because containers are short-lived
Delete all image tags with no deployment review

explanations.a: Vulnerability impact depends on whether the vulnerable artifact is running, reachable, and exploitable in context.
explanations.b: Images can exist in repositories without being deployed.
explanations.c: Short-lived workloads can still be exploitable while running.
explanations.d: Unreviewed deletion can break deployments and does not prove remediation.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.3: Validate findings from AWS security services to assess the scope and impact of an event.
questions.text: A CloudTrail alert shows CreateAccessKey for a privileged IAM user. What should be validated?

answers.text: Only the IAM user's display color in the console
Requester identity, MFA context, change ticket, subsequent key use, and whether the user should have a key
Only the number of groups in the account
Assume all access key creation is harmless

explanations.a: Console styling does not show authorization or key activity.
explanations.b: Assessing scope requires confirming whether the key creation was authorized and whether it was used.
explanations.c: Group count does not validate this key creation event.
explanations.d: Privileged key creation can create serious persistence risk.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.3: Validate findings from AWS security services to assess the scope and impact of an event.
questions.text: A finding shows an S3 bucket has a public policy, but the account has Block Public Access enabled. What should be validated?

answers.text: Only the policy text without checking Block Public Access
Only the bucket's object count
Effective public access state, account and bucket Block Public Access settings, policy details, and access attempts
Ignore the finding because one control appears present

explanations.a: Policy text alone can overstate or understate effective exposure.
explanations.b: Object count does not determine whether objects are publicly reachable.
explanations.c: The policy and Block Public Access settings together determine effective exposure.
explanations.d: This approach controls can be misconfigured or scoped differently and need validation.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.3: Validate findings from AWS security services to assess the scope and impact of an event.
questions.text: A Security Hub finding applies to a development account. Why might it still require response?

answers.text: Development accounts can never contain sensitive data
All development findings should be suppressed forever
Only production account findings can involve IAM roles
Development findings can expose real data, credentials, or attack paths into production

explanations.a: Development environments sometimes contain copied data, credentials, or trust paths.
explanations.b: Permanent suppression can hide recurring governance gaps.
explanations.c: IAM risks can exist in any account.
explanations.d: Environment label affects severity, but it does not automatically eliminate impact.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.3: Validate findings from AWS security services to assess the scope and impact of an event.
questions.text: A GuardDuty finding indicates anomalous API calls from a new country. What scope questions matter?

answers.text: Which principal, source IP, session, actions, resources, and data access were involved
Only whether the country is far away
Only the size of the AWS bill
Only the version of the AWS CLI installed locally

explanations.a: Scope for anomalous API behavior requires identity, source, actions, targets, and data context.
explanations.b: Geography alone does not prove impact or intent.
explanations.c: Cost can indicate abuse in some cases, but it does not scope API actions.
explanations.d: Local CLI version does not explain account-level API activity.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.3: Validate findings from AWS security services to assess the scope and impact of an event.
questions.text: An AWS WAF rule blocks a spike of requests. How should analysts assess whether this is an incident?

answers.text: Assume blocked requests always mean no incident
Review rule matches, request patterns, application impact, source reputation, and whether bypass attempts succeeded
Disable the WAF rule to see if traffic continues
Assess only the total number of distribution cache behaviors

explanations.a: Blocking can reduce impact but still indicate attempted attack or partial bypass.
explanations.b: Blocked traffic needs context to distinguish successful protection from business-impacting attack or evasion.
explanations.c: Removing protection can expose the application.
explanations.d: Cache behavior count does not indicate attack success or impact.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.4: Respond to affected resources by containing and eradicating threats, and recover resources.
questions.text: A compromised EC2 instance is still communicating with suspicious IPs. What is the best first containment action?

answers.text: Terminate the instance immediately without snapshots or logs
Open all inbound ports for responders
Move the instance to an isolation security group while preserving evidence
Disable CloudTrail to reduce attacker visibility

explanations.a: Immediate termination can destroy evidence and obscure scope.
explanations.b: Opening ports increases exposure during containment.
explanations.c: Network isolation limits further communication and allows evidence collection to continue.
explanations.d: CloudTrail is needed for response evidence.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.4: Respond to affected resources by containing and eradicating threats, and recover resources.
questions.text: An IAM access key is confirmed compromised. What should be done to contain and eradicate the threat?

answers.text: Leave the key active until the owner returns
Delete audit logs that include the access key ID
Grant the key fewer permissions but keep it active
Deactivate the key, rotate affected credentials, review recent API activity, and remove unauthorized changes

explanations.a: Confirmed compromised credentials should be contained quickly.
explanations.b: Audit logs are needed to determine impact.
explanations.c: A compromised key remains a risk even after reducing permissions.
explanations.d: Credential compromise response must stop use, scope actions, and remove persistence or changes made by the attacker.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.4: Respond to affected resources by containing and eradicating threats, and recover resources.
questions.text: A public S3 bucket exposure is confirmed and contains confidential data. What response sequence is appropriate?

answers.text: Restrict public access, preserve access evidence, assess object access, and recover or rotate exposed data as needed
Delete the bucket immediately without access review
Make a second public bucket with the same objects
Only rename the bucket

explanations.a: S3 exposure response must stop exposure, preserve evidence, assess what was accessed, and handle affected data.
explanations.b: Deletion can destroy evidence and disrupt recovery decisions.
explanations.c: Duplicating public exposure worsens the incident.
explanations.d: Renaming does not remove public access or assess data impact.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.4: Respond to affected resources by containing and eradicating threats, and recover resources.
questions.text: A container image vulnerability was exploited in a running ECS service. What should eradication include?

answers.text: Patch the image repository but leave old tasks running
Deploy a patched image, replace running tasks, validate no persistence, and review logs for compromise scope
Delete all logs before redeployment
Change only the service description

explanations.a: Running tasks still use the vulnerable image until replaced.
explanations.b: Eradication requires removing vulnerable runtime artifacts and checking whether the exploit left persistence or data access.
explanations.c: This option logs are needed to understand compromise scope.
explanations.d: Descriptions do not remove vulnerable code from running tasks.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.4: Respond to affected resources by containing and eradicating threats, and recover resources.
questions.text: A ransomware-like actor modified S3 objects. What recovery action is appropriate?

answers.text: Disable versioning and continue using the modified objects
Trust the most recent object versions by default
Restore clean object versions or backups after containment and validate integrity
Publish the bucket to crowdsource recovery

explanations.a: Disabling versioning reduces recovery options and leaves corrupted data.
explanations.b: The latest versions may be attacker-modified.
explanations.c: Recovery should use trusted recovery points and confirm data integrity after destructive activity.
explanations.d: Public exposure creates additional confidentiality risk.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.4: Respond to affected resources by containing and eradicating threats, and recover resources.
questions.text: A malicious Lambda layer is found attached to several functions. What containment and eradication steps are appropriate?

answers.text: Only delete one function alias
Leave the layer because Lambda is serverless
Give every developer layer publishing rights to fix it quickly
Remove the layer from affected functions, deploy trusted versions, review invocation logs, and restrict layer publishing

explanations.a: Aliases do not remove the malicious layer from every affected function.
explanations.b: Serverless workloads can still execute malicious code.
explanations.c: Broader publish rights can increase supply chain risk.
explanations.d: Layer compromise response must remove the shared malicious artifact and prevent reattachment.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.4: Respond to affected resources by containing and eradicating threats, and recover resources.
questions.text: A compromised IAM role created unauthorized security group rules. What recovery step should follow containment?

answers.text: Remove unauthorized rules, identify resources exposed during the window, and tighten role permissions or trust
Keep the unauthorized rules for convenience
Delete all security groups in the VPC
Ignore trust policies because only network rules changed

explanations.a: Recovery must reverse attacker changes and address the permission path that allowed them.
explanations.b: Unauthorized exposure should not remain after containment.
explanations.c: Deleting every security group can break unrelated workloads.
explanations.d: The role trust or permissions may have enabled the unauthorized changes.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.4: Respond to affected resources by containing and eradicating threats, and recover resources.
questions.text: A threat is contained by isolating an instance. The application must return to service quickly. What recovery design is safest?

answers.text: Remove isolation from the same suspect host without investigation
Rebuild from a trusted AMI or image, restore clean data, and validate security posture before rejoining service
Copy unknown binaries from the suspect host to the replacement
Disable monitoring during recovery to reduce noise

explanations.a: Returning the same host can reintroduce compromise.
explanations.b: Clean rebuild reduces the chance of returning compromised state to production.
explanations.c: Untrusted binaries can carry attacker changes.
explanations.d: Monitoring is needed to confirm recovery and detect recurrence.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.4: Respond to affected resources by containing and eradicating threats, and recover resources.
questions.text: A compromised secret was used by multiple services. What recovery work is required?

answers.text: Change the secret description but keep the value
Rotate only unrelated secrets
Rotate the secret, update dependent services, review usage logs, and remove unauthorized access created with it
Delete all application logs before updating services

explanations.a: Changing metadata does not invalidate the exposed secret.
explanations.b: Unrelated rotation does not contain the compromised secret.
explanations.c: Secret compromise recovery includes rotation, dependency update, impact analysis, and cleanup of attacker actions.
explanations.d: This pattern logs are needed to determine where the secret was used.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.5: Describe methods to conduct root cause analysis.
questions.text: After an incident, the team needs to determine how an attacker obtained access to a role. Which root cause method is appropriate?

answers.text: Use only the final GuardDuty finding title
Ask responders to guess based on memory
Delete old policies before reviewing them
Build a timeline from CloudTrail, identity provider logs, role trust policies, and permission changes

explanations.a: A finding title does not explain the access path.
explanations.b: Memory alone is unreliable and not auditable.
explanations.c: Policy state is evidence and should be preserved before changes.
explanations.d: Root cause analysis for identity incidents needs chronological evidence of authentication, authorization, and policy state.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.5: Describe methods to conduct root cause analysis.
questions.text: A public S3 exposure recurred after remediation. What should root cause analysis examine?

answers.text: Policy deployment process, exception handling, ownership, preventive controls, and drift detection
Only the bucket's object count
Only the first responder's keyboard commands
Only storage class transitions

explanations.a: Recurring exposure usually involves process or control gaps, not only one bucket policy mistake.
explanations.b: Object count does not explain why public access returned.
explanations.c: Individual commands matter, but recurrence often requires process and control review.
explanations.d: Lifecycle transitions do not explain access policy recurrence.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.5: Describe methods to conduct root cause analysis.
questions.text: A container compromise followed deployment of a vulnerable image. Which evidence supports root cause analysis?

answers.text: Only the ECS cluster name
Image build provenance, scan results, deployment history, runtime findings, and change approvals
Only the current desired task count
Only a list of unrelated S3 buckets

explanations.a: Cluster name does not show image provenance or vulnerability handling.
explanations.b: Supply chain and runtime evidence show how the vulnerable image reached production and what happened after deployment.
explanations.c: Task count does not explain why the vulnerable image was released.
explanations.d: Unrelated buckets do not support container compromise analysis.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.5: Describe methods to conduct root cause analysis.
questions.text: A DDoS event caused partial outage even though Shield Advanced was enabled. What should root cause analysis include?

answers.text: Only whether Shield Advanced exists in the account
Only source code formatting
Protected resource configuration, health checks, WAF rules, scaling behavior, and escalation timing
Only backup retention periods

explanations.a: Presence of the service does not prove every resource and procedure was correctly configured.
explanations.b: Formatting does not explain DDoS protection behavior.
explanations.c: DDoS analysis must review both protective service configuration and application capacity or response paths.
explanations.d: Backups do not describe real-time DDoS mitigation.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.5: Describe methods to conduct root cause analysis.
questions.text: A security incident was detected late because alarms were routed to the wrong team. What should the root cause analysis focus on?

answers.text: Only the compute instance family
Only the number of Regions enabled
Only the color of dashboard widgets
Alert ownership metadata, routing rules, severity mapping, and notification testing

explanations.a: Instance family does not explain notification ownership.
explanations.b: Region count may matter for coverage, but wrong routing requires notification design review.
explanations.c: Widget color does not route alerts to responders.
explanations.d: Late detection from misrouting points to governance and alerting workflow gaps.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.5: Describe methods to conduct root cause analysis.
questions.text: A root cause review finds that an emergency manual change fixed service but created IaC drift. What corrective method should be used?

answers.text: Document the change, reconcile it into IaC or revert it, and update emergency-change procedures
Ignore the drift because the outage ended
Delete the IaC repository to avoid conflict
Ban all emergency changes without providing an alternative

explanations.a: Manual incident changes must be reconciled so future deployments and audits remain consistent.
explanations.b: Unresolved drift can cause future failures and governance issues.
explanations.c: Removing the source of truth worsens configuration management.
explanations.d: Emergency response still needs a controlled path.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.5: Describe methods to conduct root cause analysis.
questions.text: An incident involved several services and teams. Which RCA technique helps visualize causal relationships without assigning blame?

answers.text: A list of people to blame for every symptom
Blameless timeline with contributing factors and causal chain analysis
A single sentence saying human error
A cost-only review of the incident day

explanations.a: Blame-focused review reduces learning and can hide systemic issues.
explanations.b: A blameless causal review focuses on system conditions, decisions, and controls that allowed the incident.
explanations.c: A generic label does not identify control improvements.
explanations.d: Cost may be relevant but does not explain the technical and process causes.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.5: Describe methods to conduct root cause analysis.
questions.text: Amazon Detective is enabled for the organization. How can it support root cause analysis?

answers.text: Replace all evidence collection with unsupported assumptions
Automatically patch every vulnerable package
Analyze relationships among findings, entities, API activity, and network behavior for the affected resources
Generate application source code fixes directly

explanations.a: Detective aids analysis but does not remove the need to preserve evidence.
explanations.b: Patch deployment is not Detective's function.
explanations.c: Detective helps investigators explore connected security events and entities to understand what happened.
explanations.d: Detective investigates security behavior and does not write application fixes.

questions.name: Incident Response
questions.objective: Skill 2.2.5: Describe methods to conduct root cause analysis.
questions.text: A post-incident report recommends only adding more analysts to the on-call rotation. What RCA gap might remain?

answers.text: More analysts always eliminate all root causes
Technical controls are irrelevant after incidents
Root cause analysis should avoid measurable actions
The report may not address the technical detection, prevention, or response control failures that allowed recurrence

explanations.a: Personnel changes do not automatically fix monitoring, IAM, or automation gaps.
explanations.b: Control improvements are central to preventing recurrence.
explanations.c: Effective RCA leads to trackable corrective actions.
explanations.d: Staffing can help response capacity, but root cause analysis should identify control improvements that reduce repeat incidents.
